kvarner.note: Nine households of the name on the Kvarner, from 1626 to 1855, in two towns twelve kilometres apart. **None of them is joined to another by a record.** They are set out in the order the register produced them, with the broken rungs marked for what they are — the places where a join looks likely and is not written down. Read the mothers' surnames with care: on four of these the indexer has copied the father's name into the mother's field, which is why so many of these men appear to have married a woman of their own name.

cards.says: The oldest household the archive holds anywhere. Six children at Rijeka under a Venetian-Latin hand — *Gioannis Antonÿ*, with the trema the scribe put there. This one has been read on the page.

**Ten children, and five of them buried in the year they were born.** Mattio and Nicolò both dead in 1742, Antonio dead 1 September 1753, Aloysia dead 14 September 1757, Maria dead in the same year. The five without dates are the baptisms; the five with them are the burials. This is what a mid-century Kvarner household actually looked like in the register.

rung.text: **A hundred and ten years with nothing in them.** Between Lutia's last child in 1632 and Valentino's first in 1742 the index holds no Defranceschi at Rijeka at all. Whether these are one family across four unrecorded generations or two arrivals a century apart, nothing here can say.

cards.says: Four children, and the index has entered the eldest twice — once from his baptism on 22 November 1772 and once from his burial on 22 August 1775. **Valentino, named for the man fathering at Rijeka thirty years earlier, died at two years and nine months.** The second Ellena, born 1775, was dead by 2 March 1776; the first, born 11 July 1774, is not in the burial book.

rung.text: Giuseppe naming his first son **Valentino** in 1772, when a Valentino was fathering in the same town in 1742–57, is the ordinary grandfather-to-grandson pattern. It is the best reason to think these two households are one family — and it is a naming habit, not a record.

kids.name: Franciscum Josephum Aloysium Joannem Nepomuc Defranceschi
Antonium Petrum Nataliem Joannem Kepomuc Defranceschi

cards.says: **Twelve children in eleven years**, and nine of them carry *Nepomucena* or *Nepomuc* — John of Nepomuk, the Bohemian saint the Habsburgs pushed hard through their new lands. A family naming every child for the dynasty's saint, in the Hungarian crown's free port, is not a peasant household. Three died small: Giosefa in 1797, Anna in 1800, Maria in 1804.

rung.text: The obvious chain would run Valentino → Giuseppe → Valentino. **It does not close.** The one boy who could carry it, Giuseppe's Valentino, was buried in 1775, nineteen years before this household begins. If this Valentino is Giuseppe's son he is a later one, born after 1775, and no record of him has been found.

cards.says: Two entries, one child — Pietro Paolo, baptised and buried in the same year. The surname has lost its prefix: *Franceschi*, not *Defranceschi*, in both hands.
The name moves twelve kilometres down the coast to Bakar, written in the registers by its Latin name *Vitipolis*. Ludovicus, born 1836, lived to 1 June 1855 and died at nineteen.

rung.text: Rijeka and Bakar are one bay apart and shared a diocese, and the name appears at Bakar only after it thins at Rijeka. **Nothing joins them.** The Bakar books have not been read.

cards.says: **Twins, and a week that took two children.** Anna Francisca Catharina and Franciscus Andreas were both baptised on 10 November 1849. Carolo was buried on the 14th and Anna on the 17th. The father is entered as *Francisci Defranceschi **Regii*** — of the king — which in the Hungarian free port means an office, not a farm; and he is married to a second Bellinich, Carolina, where the 1836 household names Catharina.

rung.text: *Franciscus × Catharina Bellinich* in 1836 and *Francisci Regii × Carolinæ Bellinich* in 1849 are almost certainly **one man and two sisters** — the widower marrying his wife's sister — or one woman whose name two indexers read differently. Either way it is the same house. The register would settle it in a line.

cards.says: Two daughters, Maria Dorothea and Antonia, with no year on either. The last of the name at Bakar in the index.

kvarner.missing: Two books. **The Rijeka marriage register** would give each of these men a father and a bride's family, and would close or break the Valentino chain in an afternoon. **The Bakar baptisms** would say whether Franciscus of 1836 and Francisci Regii of 1849 are one man, and whether the Bakar household came out of Rijeka or arrived separately by sea. Neither has been read by this archive; both survive.

southistria.note: Nine households of the name in one southern-Istrian parish across two hundred and twenty-four years, and **not one of them is joined to another by a record**. This is the archive's richest material and its emptiest tree. What follows is everything there is, in order, with every gap measured — because a web drawn honestly is worth more than a pedigree drawn hopefully. The place reads «Croazia, Austria» in the index on all of these; the parish is Svetvinčenat, resolved from the film, not from the place field.

cards.says: The household the archive has leant on hardest. Four children, and the godparents standing for them are Nadal, Batta, Andrea and Nardo De Franceschi — men of the same name in the same parish in the same decade.

rung.text: **Thirty-nine years above this household there is a baptism.** Elena di Franceschi, 21 December 1628, read on the page at Svetvinčenat — the earliest of the name anywhere in Istria that this archive has seen with its own eyes. She is not joined to anyone below her.

cards.says: Gasparo's three children begin eighteen years after Anto's last. A brother, a son, a cousin or a stranger — the register does not say.

rung.text: Anto's last child is 1674; Gasparo's first is 1692. **Nothing links them.** The one book that would — the Svetvinčenat marriage register — runs 1581–89 and 1622–23 and then jumps to 1762. The century that matters is not in it.

cards.says: Piero's household overlaps Gasparo's by fourteen years. Two men of the name fathering in one parish at one time is the ordinary shape of brothers, or of cousins.

rung.text: Overlapping households are **evidence of a family, not of a descent**. Two men fathering side by side cannot be put in sequence.

cards.says: Mattio, two children, sixteen years after Piero's last.
Nadal — the same forename as one of the godparents standing at Anto's baptisms sixty years earlier. A grandson's name, or a common name in a small parish.

rung.text: **Nadal is the only forename that recurs across the whole web.** It stands as a godparent in the 1660s and as a father in the 1730s. That is either the naming thread that ties the parish together, or it is two men who happened to share a saint's day. It is the single thing most worth testing.

cards.says: A century later, and the register has become tabular and Austrian. Six children to Antonio and Maria Bergamo — and the Bergamo family marries into this one twice.

rung.text: **Ninety years of silence** between Nadal's last child in 1735 and Antonio's first in 1825. This is where the web breaks in two.

cards.says: Francesca Defranceschi married Giovanni Bergamo and had seven children. This archive once printed her as the wife of Antonius Cerneca; that was wrong, and the error came from the tabular register's four parent columns being flattened into one list by the index. The correction stands.
Giacoma De Franceschi married Gio Battista Crosilla. Two children. A second Defranceschi daughter marrying out in the same six years as Francesca.
Joannes and Dominica Clagnan, four children, at the very end of the Austrian century. The last household of the name in this group.

rung.text: No join shown to anything above.

southistria.missing: **One book, and it is the one that is missing.** The Svetvinčenat marriage register covers 1581–1589 and 1622–1623, and then nothing until 1762. Every join on this page falls inside that hole. If a second copy of the seventeenth-century marriages survives — in the bishop's archive at Poreč, or among the Venetian provveditore's papers — this web becomes a tree in a week. If it does not, these nine households stay nine households, and the archive should go on saying so.
